We discuss the results from the combined IRAC and MIPS c2d Spitzer Legacy observations of the Serpens star-forming region. In particular we present a set of criteria for isolating bona fide young stellar objects, YSO's, from the extensive background contamination by extra-galactic objects. We then discuss the properties of the resulting high confidence set of YSO's. We find 235 such objects in the 0.85 deg^2 field that was covered with both IRAC and MIPS. An additional set of 51 lower confidence YSO's outside this area is identified from the MIPS data combined with 2MASS photometry. We describe two sets of results, color-color diagrams to compare our observed source properties with those of theoretical models for star/disk/envelope systems and our own modeling of the subset of our objects that appear to be star+disks. These objects exhibit a very wide range of disk properties, from many that can be fit with actively accreting disks to some with both passive disks and even possibly debris disks. We find that the luminosity function of YSO's in Serpens extends down to at least a few x .001 Lsun or lower for an assumed distance of 260 pc. The lower limit may be set by our inability to distinguish YSO's from extra-galactic sources more than by the lack of YSO's at very low luminosities. A spatial clustering analysis shows that the nominally less-evolved YSO's are more highly clustered than the later stages and that the background extra-galactic population can be fit by the same two-point correlation function as seen in other extra-galactic studies. We also present a table of matches between several previous infrared and X-ray studies of the Serpens YSO population and our Spitzer data set.

# Young Stellar Objects in the Serpens Star-Forming Region: A Spitzer Study

## Overview and Methodology

This study combines infrared observations from the IRAC (Infrared Array Camera) and MIPS (Multiband Imaging Photometer for Spitzer) instruments, collected as part of the c2d (Cores to Disks) Spitzer Legacy program, to investigate the Serpens star-forming region. A central challenge in identifying young stellar objects (YSOs) in this region is the substantial contamination from extra-galactic background sources, which can mimic the infrared signatures of genuine young stars. To address this, the study establishes robust criteria for distinguishing authentic YSOs from this pervasive background population, enabling a reliable census of the region's young stellar content.

## Identification of Young Stellar Objects

Within the 0.85 deg² field covered by both the IRAC and MIPS instruments, the researchers identified 235 high-confidence YSOs. To extend the survey beyond this overlapping region, they supplemented their analysis with MIPS and 2MASS (Two Micron All Sky Survey) data, which allowed for the identification of an additional 51 lower-confidence YSOs located outside the primary field. This dual approach maximizes the spatial coverage of the survey while maintaining transparency about the varying levels of confidence associated with different detections.

## Disk Properties and Evolutionary States

Through the analysis of color-color diagrams combined with detailed spectral energy distribution modeling, the study reveals that the star+disk objects display a broad diversity of disk properties. This range spans from actively accreting disks, characteristic of the earliest and most active phases of stellar development, to passive disks and possibly debris disks, which represent more evolved and quiescent stages. This wide variety indicates that Serpens hosts young stellar objects at multiple points along the evolutionary sequence of circumstellar disk development.

## The Luminosity Function

The luminosity function derived for the Serpens YSOs extends down to at least a few thousandths of a solar luminosity, demonstrating the survey's sensitivity to very low-luminosity objects. Importantly, this lower limit is likely not a physical boundary of the underlying population but is instead set by observational constraints—specifically, the increasing difficulty of reliably separating faint YSOs from extra-galactic sources at the lowest luminosities. This distinction highlights the ongoing challenge that background contamination poses even for well-designed surveys.

## Spatial Clustering and Evolutionary Trends

A spatial clustering analysis provides insight into the dynamical and evolutionary structure of the region. The results show that less-evolved YSOs are more highly clustered than their more evolved counterparts, consistent with the expectation that young stars gradually disperse from their birth sites as they age. In contrast, the background extra-galactic population follows the same two-point correlation function observed in other independent studies, providing an important validation of the methodology and confirming that the identified background sources behave consistently with known extra-galactic distributions.

# Young Stellar Objects in the Serpens Star-Forming Region: A Spitzer c2d Legacy Study

## Introduction

The Serpens molecular cloud is one of the most active nearby regions of low-mass star formation, making it an ideal laboratory for studying the earliest phases of stellar evolution. Understanding how stars form requires the identification and characterization of young stellar objects (YSOs) across their full range of evolutionary stages, from deeply embedded protostars to more evolved pre-main-sequence stars surrounded by remnant circumstellar disks. Infrared observations are particularly powerful for this purpose because young objects are typically enshrouded in dust that reprocesses stellar radiation into thermal emission at mid- and far-infrared wavelengths.

## Observations and Methodology

In this study, we combine imaging data from two instruments aboard the *Spitzer Space Telescope*: the Infrared Array Camera (IRAC), which provides photometry at 3.6, 4.5, 5.8, and 8.0 microns, and the Multiband Imaging Photometer for Spitzer (MIPS), which extends coverage to 24 and 70 microns. These observations were obtained as part of the "From Molecular Cores to Planet-Forming Disks" (c2d) Spitzer Legacy program, which was specifically designed to survey nearby star-forming regions with high sensitivity and uniform coverage.

A central challenge in identifying young stellar objects is distinguishing them from the substantial population of background contaminants—particularly star-forming galaxies and active galactic nuclei—whose infrared colors can mimic those of embedded YSOs. To address this, we developed a set of quantitative selection criteria based on the combined infrared photometry. By analyzing the distribution of sources in multiple color-color and color-magnitude spaces, and by calibrating our expectations against extragalactic control fields, we constructed a probabilistic method to separate genuine cloud members from the extensive extragalactic background contamination.

## Characterization of the YSO Population

Once candidate young stellar objects were identified, we characterized their physical properties using color-color diagrams and spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling. The slope and shape of each object's infrared SED provide diagnostic information about the presence, geometry, and evolutionary state of its circumstellar material. By comparing the observed SEDs to disk and envelope models, we classified the sources into evolutionary categories and derived estimates of their disk properties and luminosities.

## Results

Our analysis identified 235 high-confidence young stellar objects within the Serpens region. These objects display a remarkably wide range of disk properties, reflecting the diversity of evolutionary stages present in the cloud—from objects with massive, optically thick envelopes to those retaining only tenuous disks. The luminosity function of the sample extends to very faint levels, reaching down to just a few thousandths of a solar luminosity. This sensitivity to extremely low-luminosity objects allows us to probe the population of substellar and very-low-mass young objects that would be inaccessible to shallower surveys.

A particularly significant finding concerns the spatial distribution of the YSOs as a function of their evolutionary state. We find that less-evolved young stellar objects—those still embedded in dense material—are more strongly spatially clustered than their more evolved counterparts. As objects age and disperse their natal envelopes, they appear to become progressively more distributed throughout the region. This trend is consistent with a picture in which stars form in the densest concentrations of gas and gradually migrate away from their birth sites over time, providing observational insight into the dynamical evolution of young stellar populations.

## Conclusion

By combining the sensitivity and wavelength coverage of the Spitzer c2d Legacy observations with carefully developed selection criteria, this study delivers a robust census of young stellar objects in the Serpens star-forming region. The resulting catalog of 235 high-confidence YSOs, together with the characterization of their disk properties, luminosity function, and spatial clustering, offers a comprehensive view of low-mass star formation in this region and establishes a foundation for future investigations of stellar and disk evolution.

# The Spitzer Space Telescope and Its Infrared Instruments

## Introduction

The Spitzer Space Telescope, launched by NASA on August 25, 2003, represented one of the great observatories designed to explore the universe in infrared light. As part of NASA's Great Observatories program—alongside the Hubble Space Telescope, the Chandra X-ray Observatory, and the Compton Gamma Ray Observatory—Spitzer opened a new window into cosmic phenomena that are invisible to the human eye. Central to its scientific capabilities were its onboard instruments, most notably IRAC and MIPS.

## Understanding Infrared Astronomy

Infrared radiation is emitted by objects that are too cool or too obscured to be seen in visible light. Dust clouds, forming stars, distant galaxies, and even planetary bodies emit strongly in the infrared. By observing at these wavelengths, Spitzer allowed astronomers to peer through cosmic dust and study regions of the universe that remained hidden from optical telescopes.

## IRAC: The Infrared Array Camera

The Infrared Array Camera (IRAC) was one of Spitzer's primary instruments. IRAC operated at four wavelengths: 3.6, 4.5, 5.8, and 8.0 micrometers. This versatile camera captured detailed images across these bands simultaneously, making it invaluable for a wide range of studies.

IRAC was particularly useful for:
- Investigating the formation of stars and planetary systems
- Studying distant galaxies in the early universe
- Mapping the structure of our own Milky Way
- Detecting brown dwarfs and other faint objects

Notably, IRAC continued to function during Spitzer's "warm mission" phase, which began after the telescope's coolant was depleted in 2009. Two of its four channels remained operational, extending the instrument's scientific productivity for years.

## MIPS: The Multiband Imaging Photometer

The Multiband Imaging Photometer for Spitzer (MIPS) complemented IRAC by observing at longer wavelengths: 24, 70, and 160 micrometers. These far-infrared observations were crucial for studying cooler objects and processes.

MIPS enabled astronomers to:
- Examine cold dust in galaxies and star-forming regions
- Study the debris disks around stars that may indicate planet formation
- Investigate the thermal emission from distant, dusty galaxies
- Map large-scale structures of interstellar material

Because it operated at longer wavelengths, MIPS required extremely cold conditions and relied heavily on Spitzer's cryogenic cooling system.

## The Importance of Cooling

Both instruments depended on keeping the telescope exceptionally cold. Infrared observations are easily contaminated by heat from the instrument itself. Spitzer carried a supply of liquid helium to cool its detectors to just a few degrees above absolute zero. When this coolant ran out in May 2009, MIPS ceased operations, while IRAC's shorter wavelength channels continued in the warm mission.

## Legacy

The Spitzer Space Telescope operated for more than 16 years before being decommissioned in January 2020. Through the combined power of IRAC and MIPS, Spitzer transformed our understanding of the cosmos—from nearby exoplanets to the most distant galaxies. Its data continues to be studied by researchers today, ensuring that its scientific legacy endures well beyond the mission's end.

## Conclusion

IRAC and MIPS were the eyes through which Spitzer revealed the hidden infrared universe. Together, they demonstrated the power of space-based infrared astronomy and paved the way for future missions, including the James Webb Space Telescope. The discoveries enabled by these instruments remain a testament to the enduring value of exploring the cosmos across the entire electromagnetic spectrum.

The relatively high fraction of embedded protostars, together with the compact spatial distribution, suggests that Serpens is a young and dynamically active region undergoing a recent burst of star formation. # YSO Identification in Serpens Using Spitzer IRAC/MIPS Data

## Key Findings Summary

Studies using Spitzer's IRAC (3.6–8.0 μm) and MIPS (24, 70 μm) instruments to survey the Serpens Molecular Cloud have contributed significantly to our understanding of young stellar object (YSO) populations. Here are the typical key findings from such work (notably work by Harvey et al. 2006, 2007 as part of the Spitzer "Cores to Disks" c2d Legacy program):

## Source Identification and Classification

- **Infrared excess as a discriminator**: YSOs were identified primarily through their **infrared excess emission** in the mid-IR, which distinguishes them from reddened background stars that follow simple stellar photospheres.

- **Color-color and color-magnitude diagrams**: Combining IRAC and MIPS bands allowed placement of sources in multi-dimensional color space, where YSOs occupy distinct regions from field stars.

## Distinguishing Extragalactic Contaminants

- **Background galaxies problem**: Star-forming galaxies and AGN can mimic YSO colors because they also show red mid-IR colors from PAH emission and dust.

- **Empirical separation criteria**: The c2d team developed probability-based classification schemes using both **color and brightness (flux)**. Extragalactic sources are typically **fainter** at 24 μm, so magnitude cuts effectively separated them from genuine (brighter) cluster YSOs.

- **Comparison with off-cloud/control fields**: Extragalactic contamination rates were estimated using data from fields outside the cloud (like the SWIRE survey) to statistically characterize the background population.

## Physical Characterization of YSOs

- **Evolutionary classification**: Sources were sorted into Class I (embedded protostars), Flat-spectrum, Class II (T Tauri stars with disks), and Class III (weak-disk/diskless) based on their **spectral energy distribution (SED) slopes**.

- **High star-formation efficiency**: Serpens was found to be a relatively **dense, active, and young** star-forming region with a high concentration of embedded, early-stage objects.

- **Spatial clustering**: YSOs were found to be strongly clustered, correlating with dense molecular gas, while contaminants were more uniformly distributed.

---

# Abstract

We present a comprehensive census of the young stellar object (YSO) population in the Serpens Molecular Cloud, combining multi-wavelength photometry from *Spitzer* (IRAC and MIPS), *Herschel*, near-infrared surveys (2MASS, UKIDSS), and *Gaia* astrometry. To isolate genuine cloud members from foreground stars and extragalactic contaminants, we employ a multi-stage classification scheme. Candidate YSOs were first selected via infrared color-color and color-magnitude diagrams, then refined using spectral index measurements ([3.6]–[24]) across the 2–24 μm range. Contamination from star-forming galaxies, unresolved AGN, and reddened background giants was mitigated through magnitude cuts, PAH-emission diagnostics, and parallax/proper-motion consistency criteria from *Gaia* DR3. This yields a high-confidence sample of **N** Class 0/I, Flat-spectrum, Class II, and Class III sources.

The derived luminosity function, extending into the substellar regime, is well described by a log-normal distribution and is statistically consistent with the system initial mass function inferred for nearby low-mass star-forming regions, suggesting a universal fragmentation process.

Spatial clustering analysis using the minimum spanning tree (MST) and two-point correlation function reveals significant substructure, with the youngest (Class 0/I) sources exhibiting the strongest clustering and tightest association with dense gas filaments traced by *Herschel* column-density maps. More evolved (Class II/III) objects show progressively dispersed, less-correlated distributions, consistent with dynamical evolution and drift from natal cores. The Q-parameter indicates a hierarchical, fractal spatial structure rather than a centrally concentrated cluster. These results collectively constrain the timescale, efficiency, and spatial progression of star formation across the Serpens complex.

# A Multiwavelength Survey of Protostars and Star+Disk Systems in the Serpens Molecular Cloud

## Abstract

We present a comprehensive survey of young stellar objects (YSOs) in the Serpens molecular cloud, one of the most active nearby regions of low-mass star formation. Using deep near- and mid-infrared photometry, we identify and classify a sample of protostars and star+disk systems across the cloud, characterizing their evolutionary stages through spectral energy distribution (SED) analysis and infrared color diagnostics. Our survey encompasses the densely clustered Serpens Core as well as the more distributed southern populations, providing a census of the embedded stellar content down to substellar masses.

We construct color-color and color-magnitude diagrams to distinguish sources with intrinsic infrared excess from reddened background stars and diskless members. The distribution of sources in these diagrams reveals clear segregation between Class I protostars, flat-spectrum sources, and Class II disk-bearing objects, consistent with an evolutionary sequence traced by declining envelope emission. We estimate spectral indices and derive the relative fractions of each evolutionary class, finding an elevated proportion of embedded protostars indicative of the cloud's youth.

Cross-matching our catalog with previous *Spitzer*, 2MASS, and WISE infrared surveys confirms the reliability of our classifications and recovers the majority of previously identified members, while revealing additional candidate YSOs. Comparison with archival X-ray observations from *Chandra* and *XMM-Newton* identifies coronally active young stars, including a population of diskless Class III members that infrared selection alone tends to miss. The combined infrared and X-ray dataset yields a more complete membership list and improved disk fraction estimates. Our results refine the star formation history of Serpens and provide a robust foundation for future spectroscopic follow-up and multiplicity studies of this benchmark region.
